title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the ear to the words

questions.prompt: Five friends have just come out of the same concert. Put their verdicts in order, from the coldest to the warmest.

options.text: It was all right, I suppose.
I couldn't sit through the second half.
I'm mad about that band now.
I don't really go for that kind of music.
I enjoyed it very much indeed.

questions.explanation: English grades a taste as finely as a thermometer, and not one of these five says "I like it" — you have to hear the rung under the words. Walking out halfway is the coldest verdict there is: it is "I can't stand it" without the sentence. Not really going for that kind of music softens a refusal into politeness. "All right, I suppose" has crossed over to approval, but barely — that is the rung of "I quite like it", and it is never enthusiasm. "Very much indeed" is plain, strong liking. And being mad about the band sits at the top, beside "I'm crazy about it". Choosing the right rung is what makes an opinion sound sincere.

questions.prompt: A pupil had to paraphrase this sentence: "Within three years she had won worldwide renown." He wrote: "In three years she became famous all over the world, and her records sold everywhere." What is wrong with his paraphrase?

options.text: Nothing is wrong: it says the same thing in his own words.
It keeps the word "renown" instead of replacing it.
It leaves out the three years the original gives.
It adds something the original sentence never says.

questions.explanation: A paraphrase keeps all of the meaning and adds nothing. The first half of what he wrote is exactly right: renown has become famous, worldwide has become all over the world, and the three years are still there, so nothing has been dropped and the key word has indeed been replaced. But the records that sold everywhere are his own invention — the sentence says she became known, not that she sold anything. Drop a piece and you have summarised; add one and you have rewritten. Say it again, say it all, say it differently.

questions.prompt: In which pair do the two words contain the SAME vowel sound?

options.text: throw – snow
stone – glove
town – blow
south – soul

questions.explanation: Throw and snow are both written with "ow" and both carry the [ou] of home, so this is the one pair of the four in which the letters and the sound agree. The three others are traps of the same kind, read the other way. Stone and glove share the o…e group, but stone goes with home and hope while glove goes with love and come. Town and blow share "ow", which is [ou] in blow and the /aʊ/ of down in town. And south and soul share "ou", which is [ou] in soul and shoulder and the /aʊ/ of loud in south. Never trust the letters one by one: group them, then listen.

questions.prompt: Your teacher is going to play a song once, and asks you to circle, in a printed list of twelve words, the ones you hear. What do you do first?

options.text: Write down every word you understand as it goes past.
Look the twelve words up in a dictionary.
Listen for the story and leave the list for the second playing.
Read the twelve words before the music starts.

questions.explanation: You cannot recognise a word you have never read, and a song does not wait: the twelve words must be in your head before the first note. Writing down everything you understand is impossible at singing speed, and every word you write costs you the line that follows. A dictionary costs the very minutes you need. And keeping the list for a second playing throws away the one playing you have been given. Read the task first, then listen — in that order, always.

questions.prompt: The rules of a music festival say: "Under-16s can come in free, but they mustn't stay after ten o'clock." Which statement follows from the rules?

options.text: Under-16s have to pay, and they can then stay as long as they like.
A girl of fifteen gets in free and has to leave by ten.
A girl of fifteen pays nothing and can stay until midnight.
Under-16s are not allowed into the festival at all.

questions.explanation: The two modals share the work between them: can grants a permission — free entry for anyone under sixteen — and mustn't takes one away, so ten o'clock is a limit and not a suggestion. A girl of fifteen therefore pays nothing and has to leave by ten, since in the affirmative have to says exactly what must says. Reading mustn't as "need not" produces the girl who stays until midnight; ignoring can produces the ones who pay at the gate or are turned away from it. Two modals, two different jobs, and both of them have to be read.

questions.prompt: A critic writes that a young singer "has the prowess but not yet the renown". What is he saying?

options.text: She is already famous, but she does not sing well.
She neither sings well nor is known to anybody.
She sings very well but is not famous yet.
She sings well and is famous, but only at home.

questions.explanation: Prowess is great skill and renown is fame, so the critic is separating two things the public usually confuses: the voice is already there, the name is not. The other readings swap the two words round, deny both of them, or add a limit — only at home — that the sentence does not carry. "But not yet" is worth a second look as well: it announces that the fame is expected to follow.
